utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we ask the Prosecution to call its next witness, I do understand that there is an issue of scheduling for next week for 92 bis witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had mentioned that to Mr. Acquaviva yesterday. I think we're going to have some extra time next week. We have two witnesses scheduled. Their projected time was 10 and a half hours but I think they're going to be much less than that on direct. And because the following week is a week that we're not sitting, I wasn't sure we could bring in a full witness, but we have some 92 bis matters pending and if the Court were going to direct one of those witnesses to come we might be able to get them in. Again, although that puts some burden on Mr. Stewart, who I think is going to be the only Defence counsel here next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That is the situation. Next week Mr. Stewart will be in court. I won't be. I'm taking some time out because even Defence lawyers need a break now and then and have some human rights. So, Your Honour, that is the situation. Mr. Stewart will be dealing with the witnesses next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you think that Mr. Stewart could do -- have you communicated this? We do know which witness Mr. Hannis had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That has not been communicated to me. And at this stage, as I understand it, there are two witnesses scheduled and I'm not entirely certain who the witnesses are that Mr. Hannis would propose to call in addition to those two witnesses next week and what the number of them is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Couldn't we then -- could the Chamber hear from the parties after the first break so that you communicate that. Because I do understand that it's a 92 bis witness on which no decision yet has been taken by the Chamber. Is that correct, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. However, that's one which indicated we thought it would be appropriate for him to come for cross and the Defence agreed with that, I believe. It's a protected witness, K629.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I also do understand, therefore, that the Defence agrees that it's a witness who would qualify for 92 bis, apart from the need to call him for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: There's just one further outstanding matter from yesterday, Your Honour, and we can do that again just after the next break, perhaps, and that is that in terms of the exhibits from yesterday, there's just the tendering on the part of the Defence of the statement from 1993, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we can deal with that. We could do it right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We have no objection to it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not entirely certain that we have sufficient copies. The number of copies we have at the moment is, I think, three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We don't have to go through them at this moment. They're just there for admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And therefore, we could give a decision. Madam Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the 1993 statement of the previous witness. It's admitted into evidence and we'll receive then sufficient copies soon. Then, Ms. Loukas, you're invited to seek contact with Mr. Stewart so that we can give a final decision on the 92 bis witness to be called for next week.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. And I'll do that during the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine. Then, Mr. Gaynor, is it you who will examine the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's right. We're ready to begin with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Mujkic into the courtroom, because that's the witness I expect you to call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mujkic. Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration of which the text is handed out to you now by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mujkic. Please be seated. Mr. Mujkic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Gaynor, counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you state your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Ramiz Mujkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mujkic, I'm going to read out a short description about your background, and then I'd be grateful if you could confirm with a simple yes or no that that description is correct. You are a Bosnian Muslim and you were born in 1948. You are from the village of Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What made you hesitate, Mr. Mujkic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How do you mean, hesitate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I saw that you were about to correct something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My date of birth isn't the correct one, because it said 49, the person said 1949, and I was born in 1948.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It appears in our translation as 1948, so we all agree that it's 1948. Please proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You worked as an electrical mechanic at the JNA barracks in Butile from 1967 until 1992, apart from a break in the late 1960s for military service. You are married, you have a daughter, and you have some grandchildren. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if you could -- if the first witness could be shown to the exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Shall we show the first exhibit to the witness rather than the other way around?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Prosecution Exhibit number P371. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, sir, you see there to your left a map which on with placed some red stickers. Is that a copy of you -- of a map which you prepared with my assistance on Monday?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is that your signature and the date at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did sign this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you place those stickers there yourself?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And did you then assist in the preparation of a legend to that map, which is about to be shown to you now?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I signed that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mujkic. Now, you lived in the village of Ahatovici until late May/early June 1992. What is the ethnic composition of Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: The village of Ahatovici is inhabited by 90 per cent Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You worked at the Butile barracks. Is that the barracks marked as number 11 on the map?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And the village of Ahatovici is under the stickers marked 3, 4, and 5; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, prior to April 1992, what kind of things were stored at Butile barracks?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: The Butile barracks was the largest warehouse of the central military district, that is to say the Bosnian district, as it was called - the seventh, not central; sorry - 7th military district, and it was a warehouse of all military equipment for soldiers, footwear, clothing, uniforms, belts, and that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And after April --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: And I haven't finished. Let me just describe the Butile barracks fully. There was also a bakery there which supplied the whole of the Sarajevo region of barracks with bread, and also it was the main centre for repairing wooden furniture, doing carpentry, the production of footwear, a shoe factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, that's sufficient for that question. Now, moving to the period after April 1992, what was stored at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Well, there were far less goods there, because the goods were pulled out and transported elsewhere, and civilian towing trucks with Cacak and Montenegrin number plates -- Cacak -- from Serbia -- number plates would come in from Serbia, and the goods were loaded up without any papers and they would be driven off. And I omitted to say that in the barracks, but you can -- and you can prove this, there were two warehouses of medicines, so they were medical corps warehouses as well for the military hospital and supplies to all the other hospitals in Sarajevo, military ones. And those medicines were taken off first, to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Was there any decrease or increase in the amount of military weaponry and other military equipment around the April 1992 mark?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: I emphasised that it was a quartermaster's storehouse, that is to say there were no weapons except the M-48 rifle, the old type of rifle, which belonged to the TO, or rather the civil defence, civilian protection, and they were taken away first, then the medicines, then the tins and canned goods because food was stored there. There were flours -- there was flour, tins of all kinds, cooking oil, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mujkic. Now, in response to my questions, I'd just like to request that you give fairly brief responses because we're fairly pressed for time, but I certainly appreciate all your assistance. On the question of arming, could you tell me, around the -- we're talking about the period around April 1992. Could you tell the Court to what extent the Muslim villagers of Ahatovici were armed at that time.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: The villagers of Ahatovici were armed with hunting weapons. There were two hunting carbines. They were people who were hunters and so they had carbines for hunting. And also 15 people went to Visoko and at the end of April, and even the beginning of May, perhaps, 12 people came and they were exchanged at Pale from Bratunac and they stayed in Ahatovici. So they brought weapons with them. I don't know whether there was a commission for the reception of those weapons, but anyway, the weapons were handed out, issued out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please approach the microphones. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, just concentrating now on the Serb neighbours, your Serb neighbours and the Serb civilians around there: To what extent were they armed in the period of April and May 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Already at that time, they had all the weapons and equipment they needed to go to war. Because already in the month of February, or rather, the beginning of February, the trucks were bringing in weapons and distributing them to the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you referred there to trucks bringing in weapons. Could you describe a little more as to why -- what made you believe that trucks were bringing weapons.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: I took the oath to tell the truth here and everything that I'm going to say is indeed the truth. And I personally was present when the weapons were being unloaded in the house of Steva Petricevic, my neighbour, which is about 300 metres from my own hours, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And what -- from what were those weapons being unloaded?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: I worked for 24 years with the army, so I was well acquainted with the type of trucks and the TAM truck, a dajc as it was called, had characteristic features. It had a special diesel motor which let off a particular sound and you can differentiate it from the other types of motors and engines with different sounds. This dajc. So I could recognise a dajc by the power of its motor and they were taking the byroads, not the main roads. It was a macadamised roads with no headlights on. And I had my doubts. I wondered why this vehicle was coming in without its lights on in February when it was getting dark and so on. And between my house and Steva's house, there are two houses in between, all the rest was open space, and I hid behind Steva's -- Steva Petricevic's shed and I was 20 metres away and was able to see them unloading crates from this military vehicle. But to my astonishment, there was no lights in Steva Petricevic's house at all, no lights were on there. So everything was being done in the dark. The weight of the crates, and as I knew the type of vehicle used for transport and the type of crate that was being used, I assumed what kind of weapons they were. So that's how I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of Steva Petricevic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: He's a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And what date -- you referred earlier to February, but could you put a date on this specific incident?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: That was the beginning of February, but please believe me when I say that I never, ever dreamt that I would be here giving testimony. Had I known, I would have kept a diary. But as I say, I didn't take anything from home, any documents, photographs, anything like that, because everything's being destroyed in a fire and it's been 12 years since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I would request that the witness be shown the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, this exhibit is headed "Rajlovac municipality Crisis Staff." The date on the English translation is the 1st of April, 1992. Now, sir, could you look at the date on that document and just tell me what date it appears to be dated, to your eyes?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: It says here 09/04, which means the 9th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just note that that's a correction to the English translation. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to focus your attention on paragraph 3 of that document. It says: "One policeman and two TO members are to be at the checkpoint towards the distribution centre 24 hours a day to control all vehicles and people moving in that direction. The Rajlovac platoon commander and the commander of the [illegible word] unit are hereby placed in charge in cooperation with the police commander." Sir, looking at paragraph 3, what does that -- what, if anything, does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: They were the first barricades in our area, and that barricade was erected up at the bridge across the Bosna River in the Reljevo settlement. Which leads from Rajlovac, across the bridge you go from Rajlovac, turn left towards the Ahatovici settlement and the road was a byroad for us because the main road, the main communication line with the city of Sarajevo was going past the Butile barracks, towards Stup.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the map there on your left, is that the bridge marked at number 12?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: This refers to the bridge, which is marked. Just a moment, please. It's not marked, but it is next to number 7, across the river, Bosna, and up to Reljevo. But we didn't mark it here because I wasn't asked to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Who used that bridge in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Exclusively the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How do you know that it was exclusively the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Because we were told, or rather, a couple of people who wanted to go that way were sent back, and they said that no balijas could pass by that way any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When you say "they said," who do you refer to there?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: The people from the Serb units, Serb formations. Quite simply, the Serbs who were engaged there. My next-door neighbour, Nedzo Bujak, for example, was the first to man the barricade at the Reljevo bridge and his house is just 150 metres away from my house. Not metres. I'm sorry. Steps. 150 steps from my house. And he said: Don't go down there. I'm not allowed to say anything, but you won't be allowed to pass, you lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd request that the witness be shown the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, this document is headed "Srpska Republika, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serb Municipality Vogosca, Information Service." It's dated 11th May 1992 and bears a stamp reading "Srpska Republika, Bosnia and Herzegovina," with a reference number, a date, and the word Sarajevo. Sir, I'd like to focus your attention to the fifth paragraph in your version, and I'm going to read that now. It says: "In the night of 9th May, the Green Berets and HOS launched an attack on Rajlovac barracks, on which occasion they also burnt down Sokolje." Sir, do you remember where you were on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'll start with the 9th of May, because on that day, I fled from Butile. Actually, as an electrician in charge of appliances with the focus on the bakery, because bread was needed every day. Reservists were giving me funny looks, but nobody ever said anything to me. When I came to the barracks, the situation was not as usual. Nobody spoke to anyone. There seemed to be some kind of commotion. I was on my own with a baker who was making the bread. I was only in charge of the technical equipment. I said: What is this? And he said: Ramiz, something seems to be wrong today. Soon after that, a soldier came and he said Colonel Nikola Suput wants to see you. I went with him downstairs and he said: Here's this lieutenant. And there was this lieutenant who was already standing there. And he said: Go with him. Wear a uniform. Take a weapon. You'll be issued a weapon. And don't go home any more. I was surprised, and I said: Colonel, I've been looking forward to this for such a long time. Thank goodness I've lived to see this day. And he said: Well, yes, you have. So then I was supposed to leave all my tools and to change my blue work clothes. And they had just come to Butile, whereas I worked there for 24 years and I knew where every little tree was. I went to the bakery building, which was about 200 metres away from the headquarters where we were, and that is near the woods. Butile is a very big area, and there are a lot of woods. I didn't even take off that blue coat. I crossed the wires, because there were mines around the fence of the barracks. And I walked through the meadows and I walked to my house. And my house is two kilometres away from the barracks. But I think that it took me only five minutes to cross these two kilometres. So that's the day I spent. Around 9.00 in the evening, the first shells started from our area, or rather, from Dobrosevici, an area called Jaruge, which is a small elevation. And then the river Bosna is down in the valley and then there is another hill too, which can be seen with the naked eye. Cannons started shooting at Sokolje. We looked at this in surprise, because this was a baptism of fire. We had never seen anything like that. People were counting shells. Some counted 500, others counted 600. These are only the tracers that we managed to see. Everybody did his own counting, so the figures never really tallied. So I was at home on the 9th of May in the evening. Since then, I never went to the Butile barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of -- the predominant ethnicity, I should say, of the village of Sokolje?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: 99 per cent Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And what comment, if any, do you have about the sentence which there is allegedly an attack by Green Berets and HOS on Rajlovac and subsequently they burnt down Sokolje? Do you have any comment about that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was propaganda, Serb propaganda. Whenever something was supposed to happen, the Green Berets were mentioned and the HOS. The HOS are Croatian forces of the Republic of Croatia, that is. So there was a certain criterion involved that these people were their enemies, their mortal enemies. And the Green Berets were the entire Muslim population, in their opinion, that was supposed to be killed. So everything they did, they ascribed to the HOS and the Green Berets. Actually, the truth is that they attacked, that the Serb forces attacked Sokolje on the 9th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd request that the witness be shown the next exhibit. This exhibit is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Grain, I'm trying to find Sokolje on the map. Is it somewhere or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can be seen, but it doesn't say Sokolje. That's not what's written there. It's the closest settlement to Mr. Krajisnik's house. It is actually only two or three hundred metres away from his house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you point at it at the map on the pointer. Could we have that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These houses here. Then there's Brijesce, this other neighbourhood. This was Serb land that had been sold to Muslims. And this entire area had a Muslim population, 90 per cent of the population was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness pointed at what seems to be houses just south of the word "Rajlovac." And left of the word Brijesce. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I request that the witness be shown the next exhibit. The next exhibit already bears an exhibit number, which I'll read out now. 64A, footnote binder 24, 13-077.A.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, as you can see, sir, this is a decree on the promulgation of the law on the establishment of Rajlovac municipality, with headquarters in Rajlovac. The law was adopted by the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina at its session on the 11th of May, 1992. Below that Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond appear the words "president of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic, Dr. Radovan Karadzic." And at the end of the document, after article 4, appear the words "president of the Assembly of Serbian People, Momcilo Krajisnik." Sir, I'd like for address your attention to paragraph 2, specifically, which says: "The Sarajevo Rajlovac municipality encompasses the following populated areas." It goes on to list a number of areas, which I won't read out now. But could you explain to Their Honours which, if any, of those areas contains a substantial Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know that the term "substantial" will be of great assistance to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the word "substantial," Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, could you explain which of those settlements contains Muslims.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: I'll take things in the right order. Bojnik is a neighbourhood where one third of the population was Muslim, one third Croat, and one third Serb. If you look at the entire area, the Croats were a minority, but here they were -- they're in equal numbers. Dobrosevici, one quarter, because Dobrosevici is almost 70 per cent Serb populated. Then Ahatovici, 85 to 90 per cent Muslim. This neighbourhood called Crkotina is a name I'm not familiar with. There is no neighbourhood with that name there. Maybe it's Crnotina. That is just a cadastre name from the Austro-Hungarian days. This entire area could then be called Crnotina, but there is no such thing as Crkotina. Reljevo was 99 per cent Serb, because there were only two Muslim houses and two Croat houses of Dufek. Rjecica. One Croat houses, the rest were Serbs. Perivoj, Serbs. I am not aware of any Muslims who were there. Reljevo and Perivoj is the same neighbourhood. There's only a railroad splitting it up. Zabrdje. Zabrdje has a majority Serb population. Quite a bit of the land had been sold, though. So there were some Muslims there too. I cannot give you the exact ratio. Smiljevi, also Serb. Rajlovac, also Serb. Although Rajlovac had the smallest population of all, because this is an industrial centre and the barracks took up a great deal of the land too. Brijesce. Now, that is Muslim-populated. The street of the 25th of May, Padina [phoen] Brijesce, Brijesce Brdo rather, that was the Serb population. Bacici, the Serb population was there again. But this is an agriculture complex, so there weren't that many people to begin with. Bacici and Halilovici. I know about that because there's a barracks in Halilovici. This is a different barracks. Then there were ten houses there, Djokici, not more than that. Then Dolac and Zuc. That is where the Serb population had a majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to take you now to the 29th of May, 1992. Where were you on that day?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: On the 29th of May, 1992, on that fateful day, I was at home. In the morning I was in the vegetable garden digging potatoes. I live in a village, basically, so I have my own plot of land. It belonged to my forefathers. However, it started to rain, so my wife and I went home. We took a shower, we had some lunch. It kept raining. And then around 3.15 or 3.20 p.m. - please don't take my word for every little minute - the first shell fell in our area. This was out of the blue, because we certainly did not expect any such thing. This is the day when the shelling began, the shelling of Ahatovici, which went on for all of four days. It stopped all of a sudden, as if someone had issued an order to stop and not a single shell fell after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, could you see where the shells were coming from?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you something that is the actual truth. We had not been prepared for a war or any kind of war option. So it seems tragicomical, but we went to the hills to see who was shooting and who was firing from where. We did not realise that we were the target. We were not seeking shelters or anything. All of this was spontaneous. Everybody was running around to see where the shooting was coming from. We did not think that this would go on for four days. We thought that this was just a few random shells and we were wondering where they were coming from. One hundred metres from my house there is a hillock from which Rajlovac can be seen quite clearly. There were two tanks, and also some parapets. And shells were falling, but they couldn't actually hit our houses. Other shells were coming from the Butile barracks. It's a place called Tunje, actually. So towards Ahatovici, about 500 metres away, that is that area. And the tank could actually fire at Ahatovici. Other shells were coming from the surrounding hills. Mortars had already been located there. So the entire neighbourhood was being hit by shells. Tanks were firing at the higher areas, and from Butile, fire was coming at the lower areas. But this is not a plain. There are these small hills, so they cannot target, say, my house, because of the hills. But the mortars were placed on the surrounding hills and they were hitting one house after the other. So actually, every house was targeted by shells. I'm going to mention that my house was hit by four shells, four mortar shells, to be precise, not tank shells, because my house could not be targeted from any one of the tanks that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you say you saw mortars and tanks. Did you see any personnel at those mortars and tanks?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Sir, a tank does not fire from a 50-metre distance, but from a 5-kilometre distance. So this is not theoretically possible. The mortars were near the Serb houses, because Ahatovici has a population that is primarily Muslim, 90 per cent. And the Serbs were on the outskirts of Ahatovici, near the woods. And it's hilly, too, in that area. So I could not see through the woods who was firing. And of course, the place where the mortar was, was camouflaged, and there was no theoretical possibility of seeing it or realising who was doing the actual shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: From the moment the firing began on the 29th of May until you left the village, how -- how frequent was the firing?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you a joke now. We were focussed on basements. Houses had basements. So we sought shelter in these basements. We'd sit there, day in, day out. Do you realise that this went on all the time, this shelling? And a relative of mine said, by way of a joke: What is this? They didn't even have a cigarette break. They're not even taking a cigarette break. That was his point. Because this went on all the time, as if they didn't even take a cigarette break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When did you personally leave the village of Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: In this situation, when it was impossible to leave the shelter, during the night of the 31st of May, we made a decision. My house is at the beginning of Ahatovici, and the Serb houses are right across the road. So there were rifles there and shells, and we decided to withdraw to the centre of Ahatovici, four or five hundred metres towards the centre. Women, children, we were all walking in small groups of two or three. So if a shell would fall, it wouldn't hit a large group of people. We were learning what to do in this situation along the way. We came to Fikret Mujkic's house, which is in the centre of Ahatovici, and it's in a small valley, so a rifle could not hit us there. There were machine-guns too, but then you could tell by then where you can go and where you cannot go. We found another relative of ours there, who had withdrawn from the outskirts. The point was that nobody could get out of Ahatovici. So it was the outskirts that were shelled the most heavily. Of course, a few shells fell into the centre too, but not as much as the outskirts. There were about 200 of us there: Women, children, old men, and also some of us who were of military age. I admit that I did have a weapon. Then Fikret Mujkic walked up to me. He was a member of the Crisis Staff. And he said: Ramiz, go to Brzeljak. That's on the top of Ahatovici. Meho Novalija, he's a hunter, he is familiar with the area. Go towards Bioca from Visoko, a platoon of soldiers had set out to help us withdraw. I said, since he's younger than I am, I said: Fikro, this is a Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond question of life and death. So is this something that you concocted or is this a decision of the Crisis Staff? And he said: Ramiz, this is a decision. It's not something that simply came out of my head. I didn't even say goodbye to my wife or daughter. I simply started walking towards Meho Novalija's house, or actually the place where he told me that Meho Novalija would be. I went up there, I found a young man, and I asked him where Meho was, and he said: Five minutes ago they went to Bioca so you'll catch up with them, but watch out; they are hitting the area you have to go through. Shells are falling there. I went that way. There were a few shells. But the shell would hit the area a bit above me, so I was not wounded. And then I came to the woods. About one kilometre is the distance between that house and the woods. And I heard voices, and I realise that it was Meho Novalija that is going there to meet the people from Visoko. Perhaps it's already the people from Visoko who got there, which really made me feel better.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If I can interrupt for a moment. You said that you set out towards Bioca. Did you in fact get to Bioca?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Not that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd just like to bring you forward to the time that you arrived in Bioca. What date was that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: I arrived in Bioca on the 1st of June, around 10.00. You interrupted me at the key moment. The voices I heard then were not Meho Novalija's voice or the voices of the people from Visoko. These were voices of the Serb soldiers going from Ilijas. And they had already torched Bioca, taken the people to the school in Bioca. I was not aware of that. None of us were aware of that because there was no communication with Bioca and nobody managed to get out, due to the shelling. I simply hid in the bushes, and then I realised that these were Serb soldiers, not our people. No way. According to the way they spoke and the swearwords they used, I realised that it was the Serb army. And around 9.00 in the morning, I came to the house of Sehic "Iso" Ismet. His nickname is Iso. But the house was open, the cattle were walking about, yard. So Bioca had already fallen. So they had already taken care of Bioca. And then, instead of the people from Visoko coming to help us, it was Serb forces that were moving in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, when you say you arrived in Bioca, is that Gornja Bioca or Donja Bioca?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Gornja Bioca. Donja Bioca is much lower than that. I went there only twice in my entire life.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And just on the map, which is on your left there, due west of Svrake - excuse me my pronunciation - is a settlement "G. Bioca." Is that the place you're talking about now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear the witness. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if you look due west, due south of that, sir, you see G. Bioca?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Oh, G. Bioca. Yes. Gornja Bioca, yes. On the same line where Svrake is. Gornja and Donja Bioca are very far away from each other. This is close to the town of Ilijas, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I want you to describe for the Court: On the moment you arrived at Gornja Bioca, what did you see exactly?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Well, I arrived in Gornja Bioca and the first houses -- because Gornja Bioca follows on from Ahatovici. They are just separated by road. The Novi Grad and Ilijas municipalities are separated by road. So the people in Gornja Bioca, and that was the road I would take if I was ever to go walking, because I had some relatives in Gornja Bioca, in fact, so I would go visiting, not very often, if truth be told, but anyway. So I did know the houses. But when I arrived, all the doors had been pulled out, and the cattle were walking around one of the houses belonging to Sehic. And I know their nicknames. I don't know their full names. But anyway, that house had burnt down. And it was clear to me that Bioca had been taken control of and that there were no Muslim inhabitants there any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of that village before this moment?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: The village of Bioca was a Muslim village. There was one house belonging to the Brankovic family, Vidoje and Djordje Brankovic, but it was right up by the road, the road separating the Novi Grad municipality and the Ilijas municipality. But the road fork, there's a fork in the road, so on the right-hand side you go to Sekovici; on the left Durmici. Sekovic and Durmici, the family houses of the Sekici family and Durmici families.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, sir, where was the Muslim population of Gornja Bioca?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: The population of Gornja Bioca had been taken away to the school in Donja Bioca.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: How do I know that? Because they brought me on the 22nd of August to a mountain hut and I came across those people there. Most of them, or 90 per cent of the people, the detainees, the prisoners, were people from Gornja and Donja Bioca. So that I knew from the stories they told. We had enough time to talk to each other and I can guarantee that that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, the translation of what you said says mountain hut. On the 22nd of August, could you just repeat where you were brought.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: On the 22nd of August, I was brought from the hospital, Zica Blazuj, the Ilijas municipality to Planjina kuca, Planjina house in Semizovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, sir, you said that the population of Gornja Bioca had been taken away to the school of Donja Bioca. Who took them away?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Sir, Your Honours, I can't say -- or rather, on the basis of their stories and what they said, this was done by the Serb army, the Serbian soldiers, the units of the Ilijas municipality, in fact. I can't comment. I can't guarantee. I didn't see it myself. But what I did see and I did happen to meet those Serb soldiers who had already cleared Bioca and moved towards Ahatovici. So there was an order to this. I didn't see that actually happen, but judging by what they said, yes, because the 3rd unit wasn't there, the one that could have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: On what date did you arrive back in Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: I returned to Ahatovici on the 3rd of June, 1992, in the early morning, at dawn. Because I wasn't able to return before that, since there was fighting going on from the north, from the direction of Bioca towards Ahatovici, and I was to their rear, behind their backs. I didn't know that I would ever be faced with a situation of that kind and I wasn't able to break through and reach Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived back to Ahatovici on the 3rd of June, 1992, what did you see in the village?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: I saw chaos. I saw sadness. I saw houses on fire because the houses were burnt systematically. Every older house that had this four-cornered roof, I don't know how to explain this, but it's a typical type of roof for that house, for Muslim houses. They were constructed that way. They were on fire. The newer houses were not set fire to because they were later used to put up the Serb population and the people -- Serbs expelled from other parts of the country, who had come in from other parts of the country. But it was a terrible, terrible sight to behold, horrendous.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Was there a mosque in the village of Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. In the village of Ahatovici, in 1969, a mosque was erected and during Tito's time, all the necessary papers for constructing it were obtained. It was our symbol and a fulcrum. And anyway, you turned, you would be going towards and facing the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What state was the mosque in when you got back to the village on the 3rd of June?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: It was there. It hadn't been blown up then. On the 3rd of June, in the evening, or rather, on the 3rd of June, in the morning, I came across a wounded young man and I spent the whole day sitting in a bush, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond behind a bush with him. And when it was night-time, I put him out into the woods. Actually, it's my own wood and forest belonging to my forefathers. And I would often go there. So I knew my way about. I didn't have to have any light or anything like that. So I pulled him out into the woods and the mosque was still standing then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And you said in answer to my earlier question, you said it hadn't been blown up then. When had it -- when was it blown up?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: On the 3rd, in the evening, as I said, we reached the forest. We set up a tent on the 4th. The young man was wounded in his heel. He wasn't able to move around. He cried. It was painful. I didn't have any medicines to give him, just some herbs that I put on the wound. And I set up this makeshift tent. But sometime towards the afternoon, we heard a very strong, loud explosion, and as we knew that the war had already started, we weren't able to know what that actually was. Never did it enter my mind that that could have been the mosque being blown up. Now, on the 6th of June, I left around noon. I went up to a hill called Vis. And there's an open space there called Strahoc. But anyway, it's a hill from which you can see the overall Gornji Mihaljevici, Ahatovici settlements, parts of Dobrosevici, Kastela Velovac [phoen], Kasima Butare [phoen], Ilidza, the airport, Butmir airport, the town of Butmir, then towards the left Nedzarici, Oslobodjenja, and part of the Ali Pasina Polje settlement. So it was a vantage point from which you could see everything. It was an elevation and you could see right the way around. So when I reached that point, on the 6th of June, I looked around and the first thing that I did was to look around, and I noticed that there was no mosque. I rubbed my eyes to see if I was seeing properly. It still went there. In Butmir -- I looked towards Butmir and I saw the mosque there, and Butmir is at least 15 to 20 kilometres as the crow flies. It was a clear day, good visibility. I saw Butmir. I saw the mosque there. Whereas in this way I couldn't see the mosque, which was quite close to us, to me. And then I saw that the mosque must have been blown up, and as dusk fell I went down to have a better look and found what I found. Just one piece of concrete with the minaret still standing, but everything else had been destroyed. There were bricks blown to all four corners. Everything had been blown up. It had all been blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When you returned to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When you returned to Ahatovici, where were the people? Where was the population of the village?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: All the locals of Ahatovici were in Rajlovac, put up in three buildings, those buildings were never prisons but the Serb forces turned them into prisons. They were the distribution centre of Rajlovac, that premises, the cistern of Rajlovac, and a third building, the oxygen plant of Rajlovac. Because there was a large restaurant there where these people were put up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And when did you become aware that the Muslims had been detained?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Muslim population. I apologise. Could you repeat that population, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When did you become aware that those Muslims were detained in those specific locations?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Well, I had no communication, so I couldn't become aware of that then. But after I arrived in Planjina kuca, the detainees told me about that, from Gornja and Donja Bioca, because they were a labour platoon and went to Vogosca, listened to the news, and sometimes we would be able to watch television, albeit Serb programmes. And this was broadcast in the news. So they told me about that and that's the first time that I heard about the tragedy of the bus, the killings in the bus, and where the people were, our people were. Up until then, I didn't know about that because I wasn't able to communicate with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And where was your wife detained?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: My wife and daughter were detained in the distribution centre. They were brought in by trucks, and they couldn't choose where to go. They just went where they sent them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is that the distribution centre marked as number 7 on your map, to your left there, sir?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In which part of the distribution centre building did your wife tell you that she and your daughter were detained?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: The distribution centre was built on a flat piece of land, but there is a metre or a metre and a half which is dug into the ground. So we call it the basement. It wasn't right underground, but half underground, half above ground. And the windows had some black paper stuck on them so they couldn't look outside, but they could look towards the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And who occupied the rest of the distribution centre building?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You said that your wife was detained in the basement of the building. Now, do you know if there was anyone in the rest of the building?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: It wasn't a small area, small room. It was a large premises. And they were all in this big hall, big space.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you see that building when you returned to Ahatovici in 1996?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. In January 1996, I was put forward for a job and the mayor agreed. I was a secretary of the local community of Dobrosevici. I was appointed that when the time for reintegration arrived. And when we entered on the 26th, I think it was, of February. I apologise if I got the date wrong, because a lot of things are going on in my head. But anyway, I was in the municipal authorities, our police force, to reintegrate the area and to take on Rajlovac and the whole settlement, which in the previous documents were mentioned as being a Serb municipality. The Serb municipality of Rajlovac. This was reintegrated into the Novi Grad municipality, because in fact before the war, that did belong to the Novi Grad municipality. So in this distribution centre, the distribution centre is where the ceremony took place. And when we arrived, you could still see a heading which said the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac. Our police force took that down and put the new board up for Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that was an act of reintegration that I attended. I attended this ceremony. And later on I was given an office in the same building, up until August, when I was transferred to the Dobrosevici school and when the conditions were ripe for me to move there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, after your wife and your daughter left the distribution centre building, where -- where did they go then?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: The man who had the papers, the documents, and who had a list of the people brought in to Rajlovac, his name was Stojanovic Mile. And Mile Stojanovic used to work in the barracks -- the Butile barracks at one time. I knew him before he got employment there, because his father had worked in the Butile barracks. And I was in his house very often, because as an electrician, there was always something to be mended, the boiler or the washing machine or something like that. So I knew him personally and I knew his mother too. Vera, her name was. She would come into the barracks from time to time. We would have picnics together, because the Butile barracks was in a nice area of the countryside. So we would often go off on picnics. So it wasn't just chance acquaintance. We knew each other. He knew my wife too. And she said: Could you take me to the Kisikana, the oxygen plant, because my mother's there, my mother-in-law's there. They're old. And he said: Keka, my wife's name is Ismeta, but her nickname is Keka, and everybody knows her as Keka. He said: I'll do that for you, but I have to do something first. And not a lot of time went by. That is to say he said he had to go and get a car. And he did go and get a car and then my wife and daughter were transported --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, could you try to concentrate on the questions first. If you're asked where they did then go, please first tell us where they did go. And it might be that Mr. Gaynor is interested to know who brought them there or by what way or by what transportation. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond So all the details Mr. Gaynor might have a certain interest in, some of them, others are perhaps less relevant for him. I do understand that the whole story for you is one, but we are under some time constraints. So would you please very much focus on the question and details, wait and see what Mr. Gaynor specifically would like to know. Yes? Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, just to confirm that after they left the DCL building, your wife and daughter were brought to the oxygen plant known as Kisikana. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, who brought them - in very brief terms - from the DCL building to Kisikana?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Well, Mile Stojanovic, to give you a short answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And after they left the oxygen plant, where did they go then?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: From the oxygen plant, they were exchanged with all the rest of the population that was exchanged, and there were 513 persons, in actual fact, on the 13th of June, 1992. And they were exchanged at a place called Orica Pumpaoic [phoen], which was a checkpoint for this exchange between Rajlovac and the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And if you could look to the map on your left. Is the oxygen plant marked as number 9 on that map?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, you've described what happened to your daughter and your wife. What happened to your mother?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: My mother was exchanged with that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And could you tell us what happened to your sister?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: My sister, my elder sister - we were four children, three sisters and myself - so my eldest sister was exchanged the same day because she lived in town. And she had come for the Bajram festival to visit us, to visit her mother and us, with her 14-year-old son. And this eldest sister of mine was exchanged. My younger sister and her entire family, unfortunately, died. But she was not in Rajlovac. She died in Ahatovici. And her mother and son were killed in the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I just want to confirm. Was your sister who died, did she attack -- did she die in the attack on Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Don't mix my daughter up. It wasn't my daughter. You said daughter. My daughter is still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Apologise, sir. I said sister, in the English language. Could you just tell Their Honours whether your sister died in Ahatovici in the attack on Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And you referred to her daughter. Was she also killed in the attack on Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. She was the one -- one of the youngest people to have been killed. She was just 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you know whether any other persons under the age of 18 were killed in Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: I've just said that my sister's daughter, Elma Besic, was barely 15. And I can also tell you that in the bus, five or six young boys under the age of 17 were also killed. So they weren't military able or recruits or conscripts or anything like that. They were minors still.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just to go back to the killing at Ahatovici. Do you know yourself, apart from your daughter's sister, whether any other of the persons who were killed were aged under 18?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Not daughter's sister. Don't keep mentioning my daughter, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I do apologise, sir. Your sister's daughter.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: As to the underage people, no. They were in the shelters. They were not armed and not exposed to shooting. And so there weren't any killed minors, apart from my sister's daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, when you returned to the village of Ahatovici in early June 1992, did you see any graves anywhere?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: You mean when I first arrived in Ahatovici or later? I came to Ahatovici two months, five days after being in the forest. I would come in just when it was raining. I wasn't able to go in other than that, because they would have seen my footsteps, traces of my footprints. My wife is from Ahatovici and my in-laws had a house in Ahatovici. So I would come to those houses to have a change of clothing, to look for food. I went into Ahatovici every night. I went to my own house. It's my own home, so I went there every night.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, could you just tell the Judges whether you saw any -- anything which made you believe that graves had been dug in Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Before that, the 5th of June, when the Serb forces withdrew that had come in from the north, from the Ilidza municipality, they were in a good mood and they -- there was a burst of gunfire as celebration and they moved towards Bioca and Ilijas. And they were in high spirits. And I knew that in the villages there were no more people who were armed, no soldiers from outside. Because the Ahatovici genocide was not executed by the locals. They were guides. But the units had come in from elsewhere. Where they had come from, I can't say. All I know is the people that came in from Ilijas. But then I realised and I knew that there was an empty space there, that it was empty, and at dusk I would take the byroads and paths and come in to the settlement. Of course, I knew every foot of the area. And I went to look for food and clothing. I didn't want anybody to see me. But let me just give you an example. My sister's son lived in an attic in my mother's house for a month. He was 14 years old. And he lived at Cengic Vila but he lived alone for a month there. And I came into that same house but I never saw him, because he would hear me coming in or something coming in and he'd just be quiet up there in the attic. And as for the graves, I personally saw the dredgers digging the earth, the soil. And once they had completed all that, then I would go to that locality at dusk and I would see that there had been digging going on there and that somebody had been buried there. Now, how many people were inside in the grave, I don't know. In 1996, when the exhumation took place, then people saw. But I located each of the mass graves. I was -- knew their exact location and didn't make a mistake. Even half a metre to the left or right, I knew the exact spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, at the map to your left at numbers 3, 4, and 5, you've marked mass graves. Are those the mass graves to which you are referring now?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have another few questions on this issue. I think I should defer them until after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we should do that. May I first ask Madam Usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. We'll have a break for some 25 minutes. Mr. Mujkic, would you please follow Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, some time the Chamber will make some observations on how time is used, and one of the things that struck me more or less that were in -- I think it's in schedule D to the indictment, the Prosecution will have to prove some over a hundred mosques being destroyed. I wondered why we had to spend five minutes on a mosque which is not on that list. Not because that mosque is of any less importance for those who experienced it, but for the Prosecution, I think the focus should be on the ones listed first. This is just a small observation. You could say, well, what's five minutes? But it's really the use of time, which the parties are struggling with time, and therefore, I give some observations now and then, some guidance to the parties. We'll adjourn until 5 minutes -- yes, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Before Your Honour leaves the Bench, perhaps the witness might be instructed to avoid labels and terminology such as genocide, which of course is ultimately a matter for Your Honours. It's a marker, of course, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand, Ms. Loukas. At the same time, as you see, emotions sometimes come in.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, if that would be, I would say, the language used repetitiously, and as a standard, then -- which, as far as I can see, is not what happens with this witness, we'll certainly give him some guidance to avoid certain terminology. But until now, it was occasional.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I'm just placing a marker here at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We noticed that. We'll adjourn until 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Prior to the witness coming back into the courtroom, I can indicate that I attempted to contact Mr. Stewart during the last break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I was not able to contact him. So I will try and contact him during the next break. In relation to that matter Your Honours raised with me this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I do understand. I also noticed that the witness is a protected witness, but he testifying about Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if my recollection is good, Kljuc was at least a subject of specific attention in an earlier stage of this proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. It was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, I can imagine that Kljuc would be more easy to prepare than perhaps some other municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll first hear --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I would indicate to the Court, Your Honour, we have contacted that witness and he indicates he would be available to travel next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But let's first -- I would rather not like to take any decision if we have not tried our utmost best to get in touch with counsel who will have to deal with that witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. I can indicate, Your Honour, I left a message indicating that I'd be out of court again in about an hour and a half, so I assume we'll be able to come into some sort of communication at the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, the organising the arrival of that witness of course takes some time as well and it's already next week. So therefore, we'll have to take a decision soon. Then are you ready, Mr. Gaynor, to continue the examination of the present witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, just before we go on, I appreciate that there's a lot going through your mind while I ask these questions and I appreciate your patience in answering questions as briefly as possible, and then, if you raise things, as His Honour said, I'll take you to those specific things. Now, one of the things that you did raise was you said shortly before the break, and I'm quoting here, page 34, line 11: "As for the graves, I personally saw the dredgers digging the earth." Now, could you tell Their Honours approximately when you saw the dredgers digging the earth.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: That was after the 5th of June, because before that I did not come to the neighbourhood. Because the forces that had come from Ilijas were in Ahatovici between the 2nd and the 5th. So I did not come at that time. After the 5th or 6th of June, I came, and I heard the sound of these dredgers, and since I know every foot in the area, I knew exactly where it was. 6th or 7th. It wasn't done in a single day; it went on for a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You also said just shortly before the break that you located each of the mass graves. When did you locate those, and for what reason?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: After reintegration in February 1996, I, as secretary of the local commune, I was there every day. UNPROFOR came to see me. Some French soldiers, and they were very interested in these mass graves. So I went to these sites for the first time with their APC. I told them where it was and they made sketches, inscriptions, they put questions to me and I did not know the answer to these questions. They asked me how many people were buried in a single mass grave. How could I know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did - were the mass graves then exhumed after you identified their location?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And were any bodies discovered in those graves?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you about each and every grave individually, how many bodies were found in which one. We found bodies that had not been buried. We found the bodies of people who got killed in certain localities and their bodies simply remained there, unburied.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you just tell Their Honours how many bodies were in those three graves, were exhumed from those three graves in 1996.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: The grave marked with the number 3 was the biggest mass grave. We found 16 male bodies there. So there weren't any minors or women there; only males. Then grave number 4. There were four women there. Among them, my sister and her daughter and other women from Ahatovici. If necessary, I can give you their names as well. Grave number 5: It's near the mosque. We found two bodies in that grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, sir, another thing that you mentioned before the break was that before -- again, this is a quote: "Before that, the 5th of June, when the Serb forces withdrew that had come in from the north, from the Ilidza municipality, they were in a good mood and there was --"

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Not Ilidza. Ilijas. They're at different cardinal points.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in any event that these troops were in a good mood and there was a burst of gunfire in celebration. Could you tell Their Honours from where were these forces withdrawing?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: They were withdrawing from Ahatovici towards Gornja Bioca. Then they went to Donja Bioca and to Ilijas. They came from Ahatovici, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I request that the witness be shown the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The next exhibit is headed "Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ministry of the Interior, Sarajevo, bulletin of daily events number 114, Sarajevo CSB." Sir, I'd like to direct your attention to the second paragraph, and specifically, to the part which reads: "The Green Berets and other Muslim paramilitary formations which attacked parts of the Dobrosevici NZ yesterday, 29th of May, 1992, were repelled and driven out of the school in Dobrosevici, and from the Bioca village in Ilijas SO, and then they were encircled in Ahatovici village. The Serbian army issued an ultimatum to these paramilitary groups in Ahatovici village to surrender by 1800 hours today, 30th of May, 1992." That document is dated at the very end, 30th of May, 1992. What comment, if any, do you have to make about those sentences I've just read out?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: My comment would be the following: On the 29th of May, the shelling started. I said, and I repeat again, and I assert, that for four days there was not a single moment without shells falling. What do you mean, negotiations? Who could have gone out, and where, to negotiate? The communication lines were cut, because our telephone line was connected to the Ilidza telephone exchange and Ilidza was already in Serb hands. So telephones were not working. Who could negotiate under shells? This does not correspond to the truth at all, not 0.00 per cent. Just another thing by way of a comment. Expelled from the school in Dobrosevici, it says. Dobrosevici, or rather, the school in Dobrosevici, had three apartments where the headmaster lived, a retired teacher with his wife, and a lady teacher. In 1996, in the month of August, I got the offices of the school headmaster, where there was a couch. So there could not have been any military formations there at the time. It is among Serb schools. There is no theory that anybody would have been there in the midst of Serb houses. Everybody defended their own doorstep. Nobody left their own homes. So this is not the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, we're just going to move now to a period of your evidence concerning intercepted communications. Now, is it right that on Sunday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we move to that, Mr. Gaynor, you're finished with the graves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one issue which I will raise at the end of this examination concerning those who died in the village, but for the moment, I have finished, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is it right that on Sunday a number of audiotapes were played to you through earphones and you were asked to identify whether you knew the participants in those conversations?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I listened to audio recordings and I recognised whatever I could recognise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And were you then asked to offer your comments as to what, if anything, the participants might have been talking about?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And did you then inspect and sign a written record of your comments on those intercepted communications?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender the record that I've just referred to, which is signed and dated by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, there's no need for you to refer to that document again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Luke.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Just in relation to this intercept witness authentication receipt, I can indicate, Your Honour, that I have a similar objection to the objection I made yesterday, in relation to the last witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. The problem, however, is that the ruling of yesterday included some assessment of whether the witness would have any specific knowledge he could put in place in relation to that --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- conversation. So it's difficult. If you say it's just comments rather than anything else, then -- or speculation, speculative comment, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, it's something we're not seeking; on the other hand, we have a relatively long list. Perhaps we should go through it portion by portion and see whether there's anything to be added to the telephone conversation on the basis of the witness's knowledge and where he is invited to give comment which would easily lead to speculation rather than anything else. So since we only have heard your objection now in general terms --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. There's an objection in general terms to a document of this nature, and specifically in relation to various of the conversations. Your Honour, there is again, as indeed there was with the document yesterday for the last witness, elements of conjecture and speculation and not sufficient foundation laid. So, Your Honour, I think it's a question of specifically which conversations the Prosecution seeks to have analysed. If the Prosecution seeks all of this written documentation, Your Honour, then perforce we must go through them one by one and establish a basis or a foundation for the comments that are made. Otherwise, the vast bulk of them do appear as -- at a level of conjecture and speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First I'd just like to say that my intention is to take the witness through the most relevant comments that he's made in respect of these conversations and in respect of written -- in one case, a written record of a conversation. And I don't think it's a good use of court time to get him to identify the participants. He's already done that. And where he's not able to identify somebody, that's recorded here. Where he is, that's also record. In respect of the question as to whether this amounts to speculation generally, I think by way of general submissions, intercept evidence is a specific kind of evidence. Many of the participants in intercepted communications, as we have previously submitted, were aware that their conversations were being intercepted. They were deliberately evasive. They spoke in extraordinarily indirect terms about many conversations. For that reason, it's extremely important that Your Honours are in possession of all relevant information from people who were on the ground at the time in order to add context to what the intercepts say. Now whether Your Honours choose to accept the comments of some other person such as this witness is, of course, up to Your Honours. But we strongly -- we submit that it's extremely important that Your Honours are in possession of contextual comment by people who were there at the time, as well as, of course, by expert witnesses which you have also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About identification of voices. You didn't make any objection to that, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't have any objection in relation to identification of voices, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then perhaps -- let us Judges perhaps first try to get briefly an impression by going through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have tried to look briefly through the comments, and the objection, the general objection, is denied because the witness adds some context. But to say that there no guessing and speculation at all in it would be a different matter. For example, when the witness asks himself why the interlocutors are talking in a specific way and then guesses that perhaps they knew they were intercepted, that's, of course -- comes close to speculation, and at least is not based on personal knowledge of the witness, which doesn't mean that you couldn't ask yourself that question and try to understand whether it's a relevant question and what would be the answer to that question. But I don't think, as a matter of fact, that the witness could give those answers. But in general terms, the objection is denied. But please, if you go with the witness through the comments, Mr. Gaynor, please be aware that the Chamber is assisted by context added to the intercepts which assists the Chamber in understanding the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would just add that of course my objection was directed to, of course, the guesswork, conjecture and speculation. I could have no objection to anything that might place a particular conversation in context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But it is the question of conjecture and speculation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether anything is really adding context or whether where it comes to speculation.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Gaynor, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd request that the witness be shown the next exhibit, which is Exhibit 369A. This exhibit has already been played to Your Honours and I don't intend playing it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, I'd like you to turn to the bottom of the third page of your version, and that's around about the top of the third page of the English version. And I'm going to read out a few sentences and then ask you some specific questions: "Radovan Karadzic: I'm all right. Have there been any attacks tonight. Cedo: Well, yes. There have been some in Rajlovac. Radovan Karadzic: In Rajlovac? Cedo: They went for that barracks there from Ahatovici and that attack has been repelled. Now there's a build-up of troops here near the shopping centre. Radovan Karadzic: Yes. Cedo: The Green Berets are assembling there and as a huge build-up. We are expecting an attack on Vrace." Now, sir, this intercept which dates from the 30th of May, 1992, is one of those which you listened to at the weekend. And I just want to focus on the suggestion that there was an attack from Ahatovici on the Rajlovac barracks. You were in the area at the time. What can you tell the Court about an attack from Ahatovici on Rajlovac barracks?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
