utterances.text: I can only repeat what I've already said. The shelling started on the 29th, and it went on until 10.00 on the 2nd of June. During that time, no one could go anywhere out of the shelter. No cooking could be done. People ate whatever they had. We drank milk most of the time because we had cows. How could forces be concentrated when there was non-stop shelling? There was no movement whatsoever. We were all in shelters. Believe me, during those four days, no one could get out. That is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now request that the witness be shown the next exhibit. Now, the next exhibit is not accompanied by an audio file. It is a written record of an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This is a record of a conversation conducted on the 5th of June, 1992. According to the written record, it's between Mijatovic from the Rajlovac Municipal Assembly and Prstojevic from Ilidza. And in the interests of brevity, I'm going to focus simply on one sentence and that sentence is contained at the third line of the second page of your version, Mr. Mujkic, and it appears second or third line, page 3 of the English. I'm going to read out the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Prior to that, Your Honour, I would indicate that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- this is, of course, a conversation that Mr. Gaynor has indicated there's no audio file, and of course the Defence would have an interest in the provenance of this particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Gaynor, you said this was a -- you said the exhibit was not accompanied by an audio file. It is a written record of an exhibit. Which seems to refer to any other non-written record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to correct what I said. This is a written record of a conversation. If I can give Your Honours a very brief bit of background information. There was some litigation earlier on in this trial as to the -- there was an attempt by the previous Defence team to exclude intercept evidence in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And we in our filings, we explained that the BiH security services, when they intercepted communications, kept audiotapes of a great number of intercepted communications, and in other cases, they kept written records of some other conversations and did not keep audiotapes. So records of intercepted communications fall into audio only, and written only categories. And from the audio --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, I take it that you'll understand that of course such a transcript, accompanied by an audiotape from probative value is quite different from what we see here. But nevertheless -- well, Ms. Loukas, Mr. Gaynor has now explained to us that the origin is that this written report was found, I do understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in the -- was it the Sarajevo MUP offices or -- Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In relation to the provenance of this particular record and in relation to intercept evidence generally, we have listed on our witness list a number of witnesses who were involved in the interception of communication at all levels, at the micro-level and at the more senior level. And it would be my submission that authenticity as to this document should be resolved at that time. This witness certainly is -- didn't intercept this conversation. He's not an appropriate person to comment about the authenticity, but he is able to comment about the sentence in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. But of course if commenting on a non-authentic document is -- but, Ms. Loukas, I think it would be fair to allow this witness to answer those questions, and if at a later stage the authenticity might not be proven, as indicated by Mr. Gaynor, then of course that would have its consequences as well for the testimony of that witness. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed. Your Honour has already made the essential points. Firstly, the question of weight to be attributed to transcripts that are not backed up by an audio file, and secondly, the -- what would be the probative value of a witness commenting on a non-authentic document. But I think the issues that have now been clarified and the marker has been placed there and -- [Transcript read in error "[Interpretation] Federal Republic of the interpreters cannot hear the speaker."]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the speaker. We are sorry, but we can no longer interpret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, you were too far away from your microphone. But I think you said that the issues had been clarified and a marker had been placed and those were the most important.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. The points I made were the -- the -- there were two essential points that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's already on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's already on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Firstly the question of weight; secondly, what would be the probative value of a witness commenting on a non-authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. It seems to indicate that on the transcript I said something about the Federal Republic of the interpreters, but I don't recall saying anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we are again invited not to speak at the same time, which I'll take seriously. Mr. Gaynor, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, I'll just read out one sentence, and I'm going to start now: "Mijatovic continued by saying that the fighting around Ilijas has been going on for two days now and that they are concentrating on one side only because no threat is coming from Ahatovici any longer." Now, as I mentioned, that intercept is dated the 5th of June, 1992. What comment, if any, do you have to make about the sentence I've just read out?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Mujkic.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: This just confirms what I said, that on the 5th of June, the forces that had come from Ilijas went back the same way, and it also confirms the fact that Ahatovici no longer represented a threat and that they were concentrating on other theatres of operation because they had already done the job there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd request that the witness be shown the next document, which is not an intercept. The heading on this document is "Serb Republic of BiH MUP." And it bears a stamp, saying "Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sarajevo." And the date, 3rd of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I might add that the words "Serb Republic of BiH MUP" are in the fax header of this document and the actual header on the document itself is Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Ministry of Internal Affairs, Sarajevo. Sir, I'd like to direct your attention specifically to the third paragraph in your version, and I'll just read out the most relevant part: "On the territory of the Serb municipality of Rajlovac, local community of Dobrosevici, fierce battles were fought against the Green Berets from the village of Ahatovici who were aided by HOS members from Kiseljak. They attacked the Serb villages of Dobrosevici, Mihaljevici, and Golubovici. During the fierce battle, the enemies were defeated. Village of Ahatovici was liberated and is now under the Serb army control." What can you say about that, those sentences, Mr. Mujkic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: All I can say is I confirm that this 3rd of June was the day when officially, or rather, the 6th of June was when Ahatovici was taken control of. But I'd just like to draw the Court's attention to this piece of information, where the HOS is mentioned, the H-O-S, that had come in from Kiseljak. And the HOS was a military unit of the Republic of Croatia. So whenever there was an attack to be launched by the Serb forces, they would send in the Green Berets in HOS. They would declare that to their people and refer to the Green Berets in HOS. But I would like to say that if the HOS took part, then those people could not have been resistant to bullets. So you can see whether a single Croat was killed in this whole process around Ahatovici. So it doesn't correspond to the truth, because no HOS soldier ever set foot in Ahatovici. And HOS is mentioned. Let me return to the 9th of May, when the Sokolje settlement was attacked. Then they brought up the HOS again. The HOS was mentioned. So it was just propaganda to mention and bring in things like HOS into the equation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd request that the witness be shown the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, this -- sorry, Madam Registrar, but this exhibit already bears the number 369B. So for the clarity of the record, we can probably stay with that. This is a conversation between Momcilo Krajisnik, and Mijatovic, and Ljubisa Vladusic, dated the 8th of June, 1992. Now, Mr. Mujkic, I'm going to direct your attention to specific parts of this and then I'm going to ask you to comment about those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, I'm getting a bit lost. This is not any more related to the authentication receipt or ... Because the last one was the 5th of June, 1992. That's what I find on page 2 out of 4, at the bottom. But the new one now is the 8th of June. And I'm just looking at the dates at the left-hand side. I do not see any 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I might indicate that on my examination of the intercept witness authentication receipt, I think it's in reference to the conversation there that's dated 5th of June.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Ms. Loukas please speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- N numbers match up. I'm going to have to take control of this microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I now have become aware that we see internal number CD 258402018, which is the second entry on page 2 out of 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's got the wrong date, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether the --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Or a different date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. I'm grateful for the assistance of Defence counsel. I think, as Ms. Edgerton pointed out yesterday, the date 5th of June, 1992, is inaccurate. It should be dated the 8th of June, 1992. The date --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On this receipt -- on this --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: On the witness's statement that date is inaccurate. The correct date is 8th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not aware that on this statement or on this declaration, that it was presented to us yesterday by Ms. Edgerton. But do I have to understand that the comments by the witness we find on page 2 out of 4, starting with the words "Krajisnik mentions Gacanovic family," that that relates not to an intercepted conversation of the 5th of June but of the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So now it becomes clear. I still do not understand what that has to do with what Ms. Edgerton may have said yesterday, but perhaps that's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's just one further point in relation to this specific conversation. Your Honours will recall that this was a conversation that some commentary that I objected to yesterday, that's the conversation relating to whether or not some sort of nexus could be drawn because of the mention of the name Gacanovic and I would submit this particular sort of commentary false into the same realm. It's the same conversation and the similar issues of conjecture and speculation arise in relation to this conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's first look at it, because we -- it might not be -- let's first listen to the questions Mr. Gaynor will put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, I'm going to direct your attention first of all to a comment which appears very close to the bottom of the English translation, and I believe it's the fourth line on the transcript which you have. It says, and this is Momcilo Krajisnik speaking. He says: "Mirko has told me about problems with these captured men and other stuff." Now, if we can just skip a few lines. We come down -- it's on the next page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, you said "I'm going to direct your attention first of all to the comment which appears very close to the bottom of the English translation." English translation of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm talking about the English transcript of the conversation between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what page?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: On the first page, about three lines from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now it's clear. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll just skip on a bit. And then I want to start again where Momcilo Krajisnik says: [as read] "But is should not be done something? Something that is not following the rules, isn't it so?" Mijatovic: I know. Momcilo Krajisnik: Because they have released some men. They went from here. They are back again. Stopping right there. Do you know which men Mr. Krajisnik might be referring to right there, Mr. Mujkic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, before we proceed, the transcript shows that Mr. Gaynor said Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik says: "Should not be done something, something that is not following the rules, isn't it so." I'm not sure if I'm on the right page of the transcript. I assume I am. And it doesn't read that way, Your Honour. It reads: "If you find a solution, it is okay. If you do not find a solution, you can include us, then I will come to consultation. We should not do anything wrong, you know."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm referring to about the ninth line down on page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you move -- Mr. Gaynor, could you please try to be so organised that what you're referring to that we can understand what it is. Would you please at all times indicate what page, approximately what line, and then read it so that we can follow you. So you're now referring to page 2 in the English version, and the witness is then directed, I take it, to what page? Also the second page of the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. It's about halfway down the second page of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you would please look at that on the second, although unnumbered page, where on the top there appears a number which ends by 0655. And then approximately in the middle of that page, would you then please read, Mr. Gaynor, exactly the phrase you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. The core phrase, Your Honour, is when Momcilo Krajisnik says: "Because they have released some men. They went from here. They are back again."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, my question to you, Mr. Mujkic, is: Are you able to assist the Court in explaining what Mr. Krajisnik is referring to there?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, no foundation whatsoever has been laid for the witness to comment on this particular conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, if, for example, you would ask the witness whether anything happened during that time he knows of which would fit into what the interlocutors are saying, then you're not asking on what those who are speaking intended to say but whether he sees any parallel and what he experienced himself compared to what the persons speaking are saying. And then we'll find out later whether the basis for that parallel is solid enough to give it any weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I'm loath to ask the witness specific questions about events that I know that he knows about, and I know that Mr. Krajisnik is referring to here, because I think that would lead the question to the conclusion that we're trying to get. So that's the reason I'm not asking the witness too many questions in advance of putting the sentence from the intercept to him. However, if you wish me to ask the witness some preparatory questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Gaynor -- you're asking the witness to tell us what Mr. Krajisnik is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How could the witness tell us what Mr. Krajisnik is referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's exactly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, we could see the wordings used during this conversation, and you could invite the witness, and perhaps that's what you have in mind, to tell us whether he experienced anything that would be -- fit into what he hears. I mean, if I hear a telephone conversation saying that they won by 2-0, of course you could ask a witness to tell us what the person was referring to, but you could ask him whether he knows of a match of that same day that was won by 2-0 and whether he could tell us had what match that was and we could later find out whether there were other matches won by 2-0, whatever. That's the starting point. But you can't ask a witness what someone intended to say in a telephone conversation unless he has very specific knowledge, for example he was explained by the witness at a later stage -- it was explained by an interlocutor at a later stage what he wanted to say at that time or whether he announced it beforehand. But I think it's more of a technical nature the objection by Ms. Loukas than it appears.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I then suggest that the witness should not address himself to the intercept for a few moments, and I'm going to ask him some questions and then we can come back to the intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, before you left the village of Ahatovici, did you act as a host of any kind to anyone?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've already said that in mid-May, 15 of our people went to Visoko to get weapons and that 12 people came with them, people who had been expelled from the Bratunac municipality, who had been taken prison there, exchanged at Pale, and sent to Visoko. And they had their families, friends and family, in Sarajevo. And they went towards Sarajevo with our people going as far as Ahatovici. However, they weren't able to go through further towards the town of Sarajevo, and as fate would have it, they happened to find themselves in the Ahatovici settlement. And as there were no military formations in Ahatovici or logistics, we fed them in our own homes. For example, six people had lunch in one house, six in somebody else's house. I provided lunch twice for a group of six people, on two occasions. So I assume that those were the people concerned, because other foreigners, if I can put it that way, other people from outside, didn't come to Ahatovici. Those were the only people that that could have been. And let me just add that they were just afraid of not being captured again, because the Geneva Conventions, for example, and the provisions of the Geneva Conventions, I'm not too familiar with them myself, but it allowed the execution of somebody who was exchanged again but recaptured on the battlefield. And they were terribly afraid that this might happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to focus on the people who were expelled from the Bratunac municipality, taken prison there, exchanged at Pale, and then sent to Visoko. Are those the people who ended up in your house who you were feeding and being a host to?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mujkic, what date did that happen that the people were in your house?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: They were in my house on two occasions, six people on two occasions, but that was the end of May, just before the attack itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And did they tell you the date or approximate date on which they had been released from prison?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Don't ask me that, please. I'm not a recorder of war events. Quite simply, they told their story. No dates were mentioned. But I think there are written traces of the exchange of -- in the municipality of Visoko with the Bratunac people, but I don't know. I didn't take part in it. So I can't give you dates and play around with dates. I don't know, quite simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to take you now back to the intercept in front of you, and I'm going to refer you to the sentence which I said earlier, and I'll read if out again just for the record. This appears at the -- approximately the eighth line on page 2 of the English transcript, and it appears about halfway down on the second page of the B/C/S transcript. Momcilo Krajisnik says: "Because they have released some men. They went from here. They are back again." Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And the rest of the sentence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to be reading more of this intercept as we go on, but I'll finish that sentence. Momcilo Krajisnik continues: "Yes, yes. So they are attacking, aren't they?" Mijatovic says: "Yes, that's it." Momcilo Krajisnik says: "Well you see it. You are a smart man so that --" Now, I want to stop there because I want to address another part in a few minutes. But right there, what, if anything, can you tell Their Honours about that portion of that intercept?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, the situation is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just intervene for one second. Mr. Mujkic, do you understand any English? Do you speak any English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please take off your headphones for one moment. Madam Usher, would you assist Mr. Mujkic. Mr. Gaynor, I'm trying to understand what you want to link this telephone conversation to the experience of this accused. What makes you believe that the witness could do this any better than the Court itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'll take it in stages. First of all, the intercept in which Krajisnik says: "Because they released some men. They went from here. They're back again." That's an extremely generic kind of comment. And I'm not sure Your Honours can draw any inferences from that comment. Now, in his declaration, this witness has said: "12 people from Bratunac were released in Pale and Krajisnik knows about it and refers to them coming back again." Now, the issue of Krajisnik's knowledge of events going on in Pale, events going on in Ahatovici, is of course fairly critical to his criminal responsibility. That's why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but how does this witness know that -- shouldn't you then first establish that Mr. Krajisnik knew about that? I mean, how -- what's the basis for this witness to assume that Mr. Krajisnik had knowledge of those persons, or will that appear at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, the basis is that the men involved were in the witness's house, he talked to them. He listened to this intercept without any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. The issue was: The comment that Mr. Krajisnik is referring to, well, that situation, those who had been released, was based, as you told us, on the knowledge of Mr. Krajisnik of that release or, well -- my question is: If that's the basis, how would this witness know about the knowledge of Mr. Krajisnik? I mean, of course he can say: I think. I'm not saying that Mr. Krajisnik is not referring or is referring. I do not know. But what would the witness know more that would make him the person that could draw inferences that could not be drawn just on the basis of the evidence he gave until now and the evidence contained in this transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this stage I don't intend to ask the witness anything more about that comment. As a general matter, not simply in respect of this witness, I think that any -- it's our submission that no witness knows what Mr. Krajisnik knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's a matter of logic. However, based on what the witness knew --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- it's our submission no witness knows what Mr. Krajisnik knew. Now, you say that's a matter of logic. What's a matter of logic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry. I'll rephrase the -- what I meant to say. What I meant to say was that to single human being knows exactly what another single human being knows, it's simply as a matter of inference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Inferences. I fully agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That was the sole point I was trying to make. Now, why -- the question which Your Honours are asking is: Why am I asking the witness to comment on these sentences, and the answer, simply as a generic point, is that because of the generic form of many of the intercepted communications, we submit that it is important that Your Honours are in receipt of comments from people who were in the area at the time who might have spoken to people who were referred to in these sentences and who can assist Your Honours in drawing your own inferences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, there is no problem whatsoever in presenting evidence on events that could explain the telephone conversation. The basic question is whether the witness is more competent, is better able to make those inferences or whether the witness is here to provide us with information, information gained by someone who was in the area at that time, which would allow to make inferences, that is, which would allow the Chamber to make inferences. Because that last little step is not something which is in the hands of a witness. I refer to my earlier example: Tell us that the witness knows that the person who made the telephone conversation left in his car in the direction of a certain football stadium. Fine, that all could assist in making these final inferences. But these inferences, finally, are to be made by the Chamber on the basis of the information provided by the witness. And the more the witness is at a distance, the more -- the less, perhaps, the information available for the Chamber to make such inferences. But you cannot ask the witness to make the inferences himself. But please provide us with all the relevant information that would assist us in better understanding of a telephone conversation by giving contextual, relevant circumstances. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, I'm going to read out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We first have to ask the witness to put his headphones on again, because -- yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, I'm going to read out --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I request a moment to confer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm going to read out a few more sentences. Mijatovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you are indicating first the page, then the lines, and then we can follow, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This is immediately following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The bit we've just been following. Mijatovic says: "You know what, why is this part now, to say so, separated, military and civilians?" Momcilo Krajisnik: "Yes." Mijatovic: "Well, here I think we -- these women, they are accommodated, I think. As many as it was possible: Women, children, and old men, to be under conditions. And the military part --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, are you reading from different transcript? It says: "With certain conditions." "To be under conditions," you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll just -- I want to check that I'm reading from the same translation as Your Honours are. Your Honour, it appears that I was in possession of a translation which was ever so slightly different from the one which Your Honours have. For that reason, I will continue with the translation which Your Honours have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll begin again. Mijatovic says: "Well, here I think we -- these women, they are accommodated, I think, as many as it was possible, women, children, and old men, with certain conditions. And the military part, that is, for the military police, and that part there will be processed and so on. They are investigating, completing it, and now what are they going to process, believe me that, that I don't know." Now, I'm not going to ask you to comment on that for the moment, Mr. Mujkic. I want to revisit an earlier part of your testimony, in which you spoke about the detention of the Muslim population of Ahatovici. And you said that your wife and her mother - sorry - I would like to rephrase that. Your wife, your mother, and your daughter were detained in the distribution centre and subsequently in the oxygen facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, my first question is this: While those three relatives of yours were detained, were other women from Ahatovici detained at the same facility?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: When one room would get full, then the others would go to another one. They could not use only one room. They also used the restaurant and purportedly that was the best room of all because it was not in the basement, it wasn't humid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And where were the men of Ahatovici detained?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: The men of Ahatovici, the elderly and children, were with women, and military-age men were in two cisterns.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you referred to the expression "military-aged men." Were they military-aged soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Well, if a person who defended his home is considered to be a soldier, then -- I said already that no logistics, no command existed in Ahatovici except for 12 people from Bratunac, there were no other people from the outside. What do you mean, military formations?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, I want to ask you now about your sister's husband. You've already told the Court that your sister was killed in the attack on Ahatovici. Now, did her husband survive the attack on Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Regrettably, no. Her husband and her son, who was then 21 - actually, he was supposed to turn 21 within two months' time - they were in the small cistern and they both got killed on a bus in Sokolina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you know the approximate date on which they were killed in that bus?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: The 14th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Were any other persons related to you killed in that bus?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: The Mujkic family is the oldest family in the territory of Ahatovici. Unfortunately, 13 Mujkics were killed on the bus only. We are the biggest family and the oldest family there, so regrettably, our numbers were the biggest. For hundreds of years, generations of the Mujkic family have lived in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Apart from the people who you were related to who were killed on that bus, do you know anyone else who was killed on that bus?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: I know everyone except for two persons from Bratunac who also got killed on that bus. So these two men came from Bratunac were captured and killed. They were buried as an "N" because there was no one to identify them in 1996, after the exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the people who you know and who you were related to who were killed on that bus?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: All of them were Bosniaks of the Muslim faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you know who killed them?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: I'm here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Ms. Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to this question. Again, this is a matter which the witness is not in position to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it depends on how strict you are on hearsay evidence. So therefore, I would allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But of course, just an answer would perhaps need some further explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the question to you -- but let me first put another question to you. Were those persons killed on the bus, were they all males?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the parties, this corrects an answer which is given on page 32, line 5, where what I expected to be by mistake suddenly a female person was located at the bus. The next question is: "Do you know who killed those on the bus?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wished to say the following: I was not there, and I cannot say, therefore. I took an oath to say the truth here. There are witnesses, though, survivors. Until the present day, these persons are my neighbours and they all tell the same story, namely, that this was done by the Serb army. I would not make any further comments because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they ever give you any further details on why they take the position that those on the bus were killed by the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, and that is the truth and nothing but the truth, on the 13th of June, when the main exchange was supposed to take place, all for all, 55 persons were boarded on a cooling truck, refrigerator truck, and taken to Pale and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. My question was whether your neighbours ever gave you any details why they considered the Serb army to be the ones who killed those on the bus.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The bus that left Rajlovac and the cisterns was escorted by cars from the beginning to the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what they told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what they told me. So it is nothing but logical that they followed the bus intentionally. And the bus was out there in the open. It was served as if it were on a table. And then what happened, happened. After all, there are recordings. This is a forest where there were no combat operations. So it was between the road and the creek, and allegedly the driver said -- well, I can't say, but what I heard, I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many neighbours told you this? One?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All eight of them. All eight of them, sir. Because I worked as the secretary of the local commune for five years, and I kept abreast of all these things that had happened, because this was our tragedy, and I wanted to have the truth come out in the open. And they're my neighbours, and we talk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When they gave you this information, was it all of them separately or did they tell it to you when all were present, all the eight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Excuse me. After I was exchanged, after prison, I spent the entire war in Zenica, and then only in October 1995 I came to Sarajevo, and then, out of curiosity, I went to see my neighbours, friends, relatives, who were all in the city of Sarajevo. And these conversations took place individually. I'd go to visit one person and then we'd talk and then I'd go to visit another person and then we'd talk again. So it's not that we discussed this in a group. We discussed this all individually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting anything. I'd just like to know. Please proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, do you know the village of Misoca?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I worked for that army, and the village of Misoca had barracks. Actually, these were cisterns, military cisterns with fuel, so there were no civilian cisterns, but there were only military barracks with these cisterns. I was there countless times because they had their own kitchen too. So whenever any one of their electrical appliances would break down, I went there to repair the damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the village of Misoca?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: I know that the majority population is Muslim. But please don't ask me for any numbers, any percentages, because I really wouldn't want to be saying anything I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What happened to the -- do you know what happened to the Muslim population of Misoca?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. From what people said and after the war, I went to that village. I had a friend there. Everything had been mined, blown up. It was very sad. It's not that the material side is that important. They had all their property destroyed, but they survived. I wish all of our people had survived, even at that cost.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I now request that the witness be shown the next exhibit, which bears the exhibit number 369C. And I believe it also bears the exhibit number 282. Now, Your Honours have already heard this exhibit. We don't intend to play it again. I'd like to direct Your Honours' attention to page 5, approximately halfway down page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mujkic, I'd like to direct your attention to the sixth page, and the figure at the top of that page is 0322-0736. Do you have that page, Mr. Mujkic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if you go down to about the final quarter of that page, I'm going to read out some sentences into the record. Mirko Krajisnik: "Fuck, this morning I heard that the Muslims, who were running away from Misoca, killed a bus full of Serbs in Srednja. Misoca was being cleansed. Momcilo Krajisnik: "Yeah?" Mirko Krajisnik: "So Muslims killed a bus full of Serbs..." Momcilo Krajisnik: "How?" Mirko: "... who were on their way to Pale as refugees. Just a little while ago they told me this wasn't the case, but that, in fact, they took those prisoners with them."" Now, I'm going to skip a few lines to the page 6 of the English translation, starting at line 2. Now, for you, Mr. Mujkic, if you could turn the page. It's about the fifth line down. Mirko Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: What's the page? Sorry. What's the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Mujkic. It's page 0322-0737. And we're looking at the fifth box. Now, here Mirko Krajisnik says: "At Srednje they were intercepted by Muslims who killed all those prisoners. Our two men have been heavily wounded." Momcilo Krajisnik: "They thought these were our people?" Mirko Krajisnik: "They thought those were our people. Momcilo Krajisnik: Yeah." I'm just going to stop right there. Now, Mr. Mujkic, I simply want to ask you this: Based on what you know and what you heard from the survivors of the bus massacre, did Muslims attack the bus carrying your relatives?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, just in relation to that, Your Honour has asked the witness the basis of his knowledge. I don't know that the question that Mr. Gaynor asks takes the matter any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although -- I mean, what could the answer be, Mr. Gaynor, anything else than -- I mean, I've asked the witness five, six questions on the basis of knowledge and what it was. So perhaps Ms. Loukas objecting takes more time. I mean, you have asked -- as a matter of fact, I've asked that question already and the question has been answered. But let's just proceed. I'd like the parties -- I mean, although you're right, Ms. Loukas, the question is whether it was necessary to demonstrate, did you arrive at that moment or just let it go.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us that, from what you know and from what you heard, the victims in the bus were Muslims and the -- they were killed by Serbs. Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to move to the next exhibit, and we're going to play a clip of this exhibit. This is an audio intercept of a conversation conducted on the 25th of June, 1992 between Miodrag Stupar and Petko Budisa and then between Slavko Lazendic and Petko Budisa.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to this, I'm just wondering if this might be a suitable time, as I had indicated that at this time I would be speaking with my lead counsel in relation to the question Your Honour asked me -- witnesses next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could have a break now, but I'll first ask one thing. Mr. Gaynor, I take it that whenever you do not ask the witness, you present -- at least you tender that into evidence through the receipt. For example, one of the pieces of comments that might give some context is that no other incident of this kind took place, not even in the wider Sarajevo. That seems to be something the witness tells us he knows. And that's through the written -- in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The written report, if you like, Your Honour, is another means of expediting the proceedings. Anything we don't ask him about we were tendering as evidence in writing pursuant to 89(F).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you're aware that whatever is speculation might not be very convincing to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's quite clear to me now. So then, of course, if you say I'm expediting the proceedings, the comment of the witness was they speak about the bus massacre but they claim it was the Muslims who killed those on the bus. That's, first of all, it's -- you asked a few questions about it, and then it seems that you just want to emphasise the point that in the telephone conversation the Muslims are blamed for the killing on the bus, which of course, even without the witness giving this comment, would be clear by reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's a bit like using Rule 89(F) or Rule 92 bis. We are seeking to emphasise certain aspects of our evidence. That's absolutely right. And that's one of the reasons we want to have the witness comment. That's merely one of the reasons. So it is to bring Your Honours' attention to what we believe to be more heavily probative parts of the evidence than other parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. I don't know whether we would always use the time of the witness for that. If a witness has testified that from what he heard that the Serbs were to be blamed for those killings and if it appears otherwise, why don't the parties just say that's important for us. I mean, why ask -- say the witness -- I mean perhaps that's -- perhaps a bit of comment in an early stage, but you're not doing anything else by putting these questions to a witness, which might be very appropriate if there's a jury in front of you. But drawing the attention by putting all kinds of questions to a witness is not a very effective way, and of course I can say it's too early to emphasise certain matters. But at the same time you're doing it. We'll perhaps further consider how to deal with this kind of matters in the near future. Ms. Loukas, you would like to make a phone call.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I've listened carefully to what Your Honour has indicated to Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the same, of course, I think the Defence has been addressed in similar issues, what I call the ritual questions. Very often is that really what you wanted to say and then of course you very much emphasise on whatever inconsistencies you find. Of course, if you say, well, it seems very inconsistent to me, I want the Chamber to be aware of that, even whether it would be of any need to draw the attention. But of course the parties are free to do so. But I wonder whether that's -- whether the, I would say the classical common-law vehicle of doing everything through a witness is always, under all circumstances, the most appropriate and most efficient way of dealings with the matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's the beauty of the hybrid of international criminal justice, the combination of civil law judges, professional judges, no juries, and common-law advocates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When there's any time left after the telephone conversation, give it some thought, for you as well, Mr. Gaynor, and for you as well, Ms. Loukas, and we'll adjourn until ten minutes to 1.00. We'll have a break for 20 minutes. And I apologise for these procedural issued to be discussed which are not matters which might be of great interest to you, Mr. Mujkic. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, is there any news to report?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, unfortunately, Your Honour. I wasn't able to come into communication with Mr. Stewart during the break. But one thing I can do is while the witness is coming in, I can hand up the -- that Defence exhibit I referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that doesn't resolve the matter. So we'll have to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can indicate that when court finishes today, I will try to come into contact with Mr. Stewart at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What would be needed for the Prosecution for logistical reasons?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the information I have was that the witness was contacted, is available next week. He's awaiting our confirmation call. He has his passport. Victims and Witnesses says they need to know as soon as possible and they will do their best to get him here on Tuesday to appear Wednesday or Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just to avoid whatever misunderstanding, Ms. Loukas, the fact that the Chamber would rather have the information you're seeking at this moment doesn't mean that if that information would be that it would cause the Defence problems, that with that, the decision would be to deny the request by the Prosecution to call that witness. I just wanted to avoid whatever misunderstanding. But of course we'd rather first know the position of Mr. Stewart. But that's not necessarily a decisive factor.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, I appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If that's clear, then, Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom again. Mr. Gaynor, do you think that you would finish within the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's very much my aim, Your Honour. Indeed, with that aim in mind and keeping Your Honour's comments in mind, I'd just like to tell you now that I do not intend to play the intercepted conversation that I mentioned before the break. We can, if necessary, put that through a different witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And the second procedural point: I think earlier on I referred to the intercepted conversation between Momcilo and Mirko Krajisnik of 15 June as bearing the Exhibit number 369C and 282. That's incorrect. The correct figure is 292.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I will continue with this witness, if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, I want to take you directly to the 6th of August of 1992, and I believe that that's the day on which you were arrested; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: With the young man that I was in the forest with, who had been wounded and couldn't walk properly, he had started out towards Visoko and while we were in the forest, an excavator or dredger came along to dig the parapets for the Howitzers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. The question was: Who arrested you? Not all the circumstances. To the extent Mr. Gaynor would like to know them, he'll ask you. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the second mistake. I won't make it again. I can give you the name of the person who wounded me, but I was arrested by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you attempt to resist arrest?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: I did shoot some 30 bullets, a round of bullets from the Kalashnikov, from the direction that the shooting had come, because the first bullet hit me, the first round of gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: After you were arrested, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: They brought in a stretcher and loaded me up onto a heavy-duty vehicle and drove me off to the Rajlovac barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, could you please try to clarify the "from the direction." It's unclear to me the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: From -- you said that you had been shot and you said from the direction --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: -- had come. Could you clarify for Their Honours from where the shooting had come?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. That's not my question. The question was: You said you fired some 30 bullets. Is that correct? In what direction did you fire them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the direction that the fire -- they were firing at me from, because I had entered an ambush.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you said you were detained at the Rajlovac barracks. Where specifically in the Rajlovac barracks were you detained?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: All I know is that they took me in, that there was military police all over the place, wearing the white belts and shoulder straps, diagonal shoulder straps, as worn by the former JNA military police. So they were wearing that kind of uniform. The military police, the Serbian military police, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So is it right that you were in the military police building in Rajlovac barracks?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, while you were in that building, were you mistreated in any way?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you explain to Their Honours any specific incident of mistreatment which resulted in physical injury to you.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: The first man who entered the cell was Mile Stojanovic, and he just took down my particulars, although we knew each other, but he had to do this officially. And later on, at about 12.00, around midnight, 2400 hours, a man I didn't know came in, wearing a military uniform of the olive-green type. He wasn't a policeman. He was wearing an army uniform. He had a pencil and paper with him. And he asked me to draw my house for him and the orchard tree where I had hidden the gold -- buried the gold and money. When I didn't want to do that, when I refused and was on the stretcher, he tied my hands up to the stretcher, sat on my stomach, took a grenade out of his pocket and hit my teeth. And then he put the bomb, the hand-grenade in my mouth and shut my jaw and I heard something crack. And I was left with the bomb in my mouth. But it wasn't an original bomb. If it had been I would have spat it out and we could have both been blown up. But it was a training -- the type of training bomb or hand-grenade that actually didn't explode.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to take you now a few hours after that incident, the early morning of the 7th of August, 1992. Is it right that you were visited by a number of men?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was my third visit, the third visit to my cell that night. It was towards morning, towards dawn, on the 7th of August. Major Vlasto Apostolski came in. He was the commander of the military police of the Rajlovac brigade and three men came in after him. He introduced them and said first: This is the Nad vojvoda, or supra leader. And then the other two were Mirko Krajisnik, I recognised. I didn't recognise the third man. And he didn't introduce him either. He asked me to tell them where Hasan Mujkic was hiding and Husein Mujkic, two brothers, and Hasan Mujkic was the head of the Crisis Staff because he was a policeman before the war. He was an active-duty policeman. They were looking for my son Elvir Mujkic and they were looking for Junuz Mujkic too. So they didn't know where those four men were and he wanted me to tell them. I really didn't know where they were and couldn't say. My jaw was broken, so when I uttered every word, I had to hold my jaw and lift it up. And then they said -- they were afraid and they said: Well, he's literate, so bring him a piece of paper and a pencil and he can write it down. And that was the whole conversation that we had. And Major Vlasto Apostolski came back carrying a pencil and paper and he wanted me to write all this down because I couldn't speak, my jaw having been broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you know the name Nikola Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Not until that time, but the man was the president of the Serbian Republic and President Petric replaced him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you see Nikola Poplasen at any time in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: I didn't see anybody, just the people who came to my cell. So no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You've spoken there about Mirko Krajisnik. Do you know Momcilo Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Momcilo Krajisnik, his father, his brother, I know them. We would meet at various funerals, and the last time we attended a funeral was one of his cousins, Vlado Gogic. We were sitting at the same table. Because Vlado's house, the late Vlado, his cousin was close by. I would go by that house every day. I'd say good morning in the morning and good evening in the evening. We respected each other as next door neighbours and we would go to weddings, funerals. They would come to us, we would go to them for any occasion of that kind. And as I said, that particular funeral we were sitting next to each other, at the same table.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you give Their Honours just an idea of how long you've known the Krajisniks, briefly, number of years.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Let me explain. Rajlovac and Zabrdje is a dead end road if you look at it towards the town. So I didn't know the families personally. We wouldn't sit around, socialise, drink, or visit each other and that kind of thing. But when there was an exceptional occasion, such as a ceremony -- well, not festivities but ceremonies or official occasions like funerals and things like that, we would meet each other. We would happen to be at the same place at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question was: Since when, even with your explanation of what your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I grew up there, sir, and I've been there since I was 15 to the present day. I know the whole area. And my house and the Krajisnik house is seven kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That answers the question. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You've referred there to the Krajisnik house. Could you confirm that that is the house marked as number 10 on the map on your left. Could you simply say -- just confirm that number 10 is the house of the Krajisniks, orally, please.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I signed that too, and I can guarantee that that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, I want to move now to the time when you were released from Rajlovac barracks, well, when you left Rajlovac barracks. Where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: From the Rajlovac barracks, on the 9th of August, 1992, they took me to Zica. It was a motel called Zica belonging to the Zica factory, which was turned into a military hospital, a war hospital. So with Rajlovac, five municipalities which remained cut off from the town of Lukavica. And those municipalities are Ilijas, Vogosca, Rajlovac, which was not a municipality before the war, Ilidza and Hadzici. And the location of that particular hospital is on the -- in the Ilidza municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now just returning just very briefly to your detention in Rajlovac barracks. You said that you yourself were obviously victim of this grenade incident. Do you know whether any other detainees in Rajlovac were subject to mistreatment in any way?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: In the evening of the 8th, they brought Husein Gacanovic, a man who was with me, because I had to tell them where the tent was where we were. So they beat him that night. He was the young man who was with me. And they would come in shifts. One shift would beat him and go, then the other shift would turn up. I don't even like to tell you all the nasty things they did to him, but thank God the man is still alive today. As to the rest, I don't know, because there wasn't anybody else in the cell, just the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you've explained that after Rajlovac you went to a hospital. You were in the hospital for some time and then you left the hospital. On what date did you leave the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: I left the hospital on the 22nd of August. It was a Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Mile Stojanovic came, a driver, and two policemen, with a piece of paper signed by Vlasto Apostolski. I think you have that document in your document collection. And he gave permission for Ramiz Mujkic, the prisoner, to be transferred from the Zica hospital to the Planjina kuca prison in Semizovac. And that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, between the hospital and Planjina kuca, did you stop anywhere?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. We stopped off at the restaurant at -- Sonja's restaurant, and I was lying down in the car, although I wasn't on a stretcher, but I stayed there for half an hour. The driver was smoking a cigarette out in front, and the two policemen and Mile Stojanovic were allowed into the restaurant. When they finished, they came back and took me to Semizovac and plan, also Planjina kuca.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is that Sonja's restaurant marked number 2 on the map of -- on your left? If you could just look at that map, please, confirm that.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] Da.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd request that the witness be shown the next exhibit, please. And if the registrar could assign a number, I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number will be P378.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: While that exhibit is being circulated, I'll just note that this is a document headed "Serb Republic of BH, Vogosca Serb municipality." It goes on to say it's dated the 8th of July, 1992, and the first line says: "Pursuant to the decision of the war staff dated 7th of July, 1992, the municipal secretariat for urbanism, property, legal affairs, residential utility affairs and the real estate Cadastre has adopted the following ruling. Number 1, the house of Almas Planja and Miralem Planja, Semizovac is being allocated for use for the Ministry of Justice for the needs of the prison department of Vogosca, Serb municipality. I've just got one question for you, Mr. Mujkic: Is this the location in which you were detained?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And I'd like the witness to be shown the next exhibit. This, I believe, is P379.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I can confirm that's P379.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you recognise this building, Mr. Mujkic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would rather never to have seen it in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And could you tell us what is that building?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: This is the building belonging to Planja. I don't know the man, but he was originally from Foca. He had spent some time in Germany. So that's the man who built this house. It's a family house, his family house. Well, it's richly -- a richly built house. But we were on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. And from -- sorry, Mr. Mujkic. From what date until what date were you detained in that house?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: I was detained in that house from the 22nd of August until the 27th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And how many other people, give an approximate figure, if you can- were detained in that house?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: When they brought me there to that house, there were about a hundred and thirty, 120, 130 people there already. The number varied. Because people would be brought in from different sides, five or six of them. And then when they dug trenches at Zuc, people would be killed. So it varied from 120 to 150. Then there were private exchanges and people would be taken off. And they did to them what they did. We didn't -- they didn't report back to us. But there were always more than 120 people, I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, before you proceed, do we find this as one of the detention facilities in schedule C?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. In fact, I believe, due to several different references by different witnesses to this detention facility, it's actually listed twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's listed twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If you look at Vogosca municipality, 33, 33-1 and 33-3, both refer to this detention facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I found them. Yes. I was still on the wrong municipality. We moved now over the borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This detention facility in English language is referred to as Planjina kuca, Planja's house, Planjina's house. There several different spellings of this location, just for Your Honour's information. Now, I'd request that the witness be given the next exhibit. This exhibit is headed "Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serb municipality of Vogosca, prison unit." It's dated the 3rd of the 9th, 1992. It says: "According to the records of the prison office the following persons are detained in the prison on 3rd of the 9th of 1992" and at the very end it's signed by prison warden Branko Vlaco. Mr. Mujkic --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, just in relation to that, Your Honour, my version of the document is not signed. I don't know if Mr. Gaynor has a version of the document that's signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that we all have the same -- oh, he said -- yes. It says prison warden, Branko Vlaco.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I misspoke. You're right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, of course, Your Honour -- yes, Your Honour. Just the usual indication in relation to a document that's not signed. But we can take that up at a later date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number will be P380 and P380.1 for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, what is this a list of?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: This is a list of persons detained in Plano's house or Planjina kuca. My name is towards the end because I arrived with the last of them. And there are a couple of people from the place where Planjina kuca is located. There were 12 people from Onahona [phoen], which is a locality above Sarajevo, up above the city, to the north of Sarajevo. So it's not territory belonging to Vogosca or this part of Rajlovac either. And most of the people were people from Gornja and Donja Bioca, the ones that remained. And among them there were a couple of people -- for example, there was a man who was from Doboj, and he came -- went -- he was on the way to Sarajevo on his bicycle to buy some cooking oil. And he was picked up and brought there. But otherwise, mostly they were people from the Ilijas municipality and the villages of Gornja and Donja Bioca.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, just -- I note there that at number 131 appears the name Ramiz Mujkic, which is a reference to you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, did you have an opportunity to just review the names on this list between Sunday and Monday?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And just reconfirmation: Could you just tell Their Honours what the ethnicity is of these people?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: People listed here with the exception of three people, they were all Muslims, all of Muslim ethnicity. One of those three was a Croat. I saw another name here, that of Zoran Blagojevic. But he was a prison guard, in actual fact. And in his spare time, he happened to injure someone. There was a settling of accounts and the other man was wounded. He was brought in for just one night but he spent the night on the floor up above and was taken to Kula. It appeared that he had actually killed this other man. I can't confirm that, but his name is mentioned there. But he was in fact a prison guard. He was a young man, highly communicative.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mujkic, I want to talk about work obligations of prisoners at Planjina kuca. Is it right that some prisoners were taken out of the house in order to perform work obligations?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Everybody who was able to work, went. I'm the only person who, during those two months and five days, did not go out anywhere, because I was lying down. I had been wounded and I wasn't able to move. And there were some ten elderly persons who were not fit to work. They didn't go either. All the rest went to either dig trenches at Zuc or cut down trees in the forest or carry the logs up to the story above. Anyway, the building was empty during the day mostly and at night everybody would be brought back to Planjina kuca.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you said that everyone would be brought back. Were there some instances in which people who left for work duty did not in fact return at the end of the day?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That did happen. Unfortunately, many people were killed at Zuc, because they were told to dig communicating trenches right up at the front line of the Bosnian army and they were hit doing that. So a lot of people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I think that in the list over the weekend you identified a number of names of people who -- who did not come back after being taken away for trench-digging duties. Now, there's no need to go through the precise names, but could you give Their Honours an idea of how many people went for trench-digging duties and did not return to Planjina kuca.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: It wasn't just one day, but on one day, one person would be killed, another day, two people. On one particular day, five people were killed on that single day. And there was a Vojvoda Bozur who originally came from Vogosca who was killed and then at Zuc five people were killed. Whether they were sent as a human shield or whether they were killed in some other way, I don't know, because I wasn't up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, what personnel were employed as guards at Planjina kuca? Can you describe who they were? Not their names; simply the -- what -- who they were in generic terms.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: They were of Serb ethnicity. There was a Montenegrin among them. I never said that a whole people were the same or equal. There were good people, of course, and the gentleman mentioned here as a prisoner, he never failed to come up to me and give me a cigarette. Zoran Blagojevic, for example. And this Montenegrin, he would always ask me whether they were coming in to dress my wounds. If he had a cigarette he would bring it in to me. But they were in a crisis too. They did have the money but they didn't have cigarettes to buy. So their conduct was relatively proper while I was there, so I can't tell lies and say they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, just moving on to instances where detainees were mistreated. Do you recall any specific incidents, and if you do, could you just take -- describe for Their Honours any specific incident of mistreatment at Plano's house. If you need time for this, you will have time.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: No. I don't need anything. No, I don't need time. I just said that these people were quite proper in their conduct, the ones who were guards. But the problem was Friday evening, Saturday evening, because the Chetniks coming in from Serbia had a weekend, came for the weekend. And they would come in drunk at around midnight. They were sort of weekend Chetniks. And then they would take it out on us. They would beat us. I know we don't have much time, but perhaps I could give you an illustration of the inhumane conduct and what they made us do. And this happened every Friday and Saturday, not Sunday, because on Sundays they would leave and go home. But Fridays and Saturdays we were terrified like sheep before the slaughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You said that you could give an illustration of inhumane conduct. I think Their Honours would just appreciate one or two incidents of specific inhumane conduct, if you could address them to the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: I can tell you about that. It's the whole truth. The man who did this is still alive, thank God, but it was a general rule that if some unknown person from outside came in and if the warden came in, we'd all have to get up, whether we were asleep or not, and then there was a circle that we made around him. It was always a room with 120 people in it. Anyway, a group of weekend Chetniks came in and they were looking around, and they used their rifle butts to hit people. And one of them said to Mirsad Sehic, a man called Mirsad Sehic: Are you hungry? And he looked at him and he said: Yes. Are you hungry? I'm asking you. And the man said: Yes, I am. He took a tin, which we used as an ashtray to put our cigarettes out. He threw the butts, cigarette butts out of that ashtray then he said: Go on, eat. They told to him eat the cigarette butts that were in the ashtray. And he said: Fuck your balija mother. Eat it. The man took two of the cigarette ends and started chewing them. Now, you judge for yourselves whether this was reasonable. When this young man tried to swallow the cigarette ends, he wasn't able to swallow them, and this other Chetnik said: Well, let the man drink something. He can't eat these dry cigarette ends. And then he said he said to the other man: Take your pants off. The man took his pants off. And I don't like to say what happened. But he said: Do a blow job and wet your throat. And to make the tragedy even worse, his father was there and all the man could do was drop down to the floor. I don't know -- I thought these were not humans. They were inhuman people who had been sent there to be killed. Because I think every state and country would be happy to see the backs of people like that. So that's what I thought. They wanted to get rid of them. But this happened several times. And they always like to think up something that hadn't been thought up before, and the people who thought up these new kinds of torture were considered to be heroes. That's one example. Another example is this: They turned up one night, one evening, and they were looking around and we were standing round in a circle. I was sitting on a table, I wasn't able to get up, and he just said to one of the men: You. You, can you swim? Do you know how to swim? And he said: Yes. And he said: Well, we'll check that out now. And he said to the guard: Open the balcony doors. And you saw the picture of the house. There's a garage down at the bottom. And then the first floor is at one and a half metres above that. And the guard was told to open the door and the man was told to take his clothes off, take his pants off, so he was naked as nature intended, as they say. And then he was told to climb up onto the fence and he told him to jump, to dive down, to see if he could swim. The young man jumped, but he didn't jump head first. He jumped leg first. And there was rubble down at the bottom and he said: You balija. That's not the way you dive into water. So get up onto the fence again.
